ai_summary: Current operations across the British transmission system reveal a stark regional contrast in power delivery and grid decarbonisation. Great Britain’s total wind output currently stands at 4.6 GW, with Scottish wind generation contributing an estimated 1.7 GW, representing just 16.8% of Scotland’s installed wind capacity. While Scotland maintains an ultra-clean carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, severe transmission bottlenecks keep the wider GB-wide carbon intensity elevated at 168 gCO2/kWh. Due to cross-border export limits, 52.3 GWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring an immediate constraint cost of about £1,702,019. Annualising this daily expenditure indicates an estimated yearly curtailment cost of £621 million, which increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £2/MWh. To compensate for this stranded zero-carbon power south of the boundary, thermal plants have burned an estimated 9,928,982 m3 of natural gas elsewhere. This replacement generation has needlessly added 18,290 tonnes of CO2 to the atmosphere today, illustrating the critical environmental and consumer cost of national network bottlenecks.
